AUS.story:
In late 1975 the Catholic Bishop of Ballarat, Ronald Mulkearns, knew that one of his priests, Gerald Ridsdale, was abusing children. He did not go to the police. He kept giving Ridsdale new parishes: Mildura, Swan Hill, Warrnambool, Apollo Bay, Edenhope, Mortlake, then Sydney, about 13 postings between 1962 and 1991. A police officer accepted the bishop's promise to handle it. Ridsdale was first convicted in 1993, 18 years after the bishop knew, and was eventually convicted of abusing more than 70 children. In 1972, in the same diocese, a senior police officer had offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day. The Royal Commission's 2017 Ballarat report called the bishop's failure "catastrophic".

Moving people away was the usual answer. In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, Melbourne's Adass Israel School paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for headmistress Malka Leifer before police were told. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences. In Israel, deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured staff to change psychiatric evaluations so she would look unfit for extradition; he later pleaded guilty to breach of trust. She was extradited in January 2021 and convicted of 18 charges in April 2023. Brother Bernard McGrath came the other way, transferred from New Zealand after 1977 allegations; he has been convicted of more than 100 offences in both countries. In 1999 Brian Houston, national president of the Assemblies of God, learned his father, Pastor Frank Houston, had abused a boy; the Royal Commission found he and the national executive did not tell police. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.

The government did its own taking. Under policies from about 1910 to 1970, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were removed from their families; the 1997 Bringing Them Home report estimated between one in three and one in ten were taken. From the late 1950s to the 1970s, tens of thousands of babies of unmarried mothers were taken for adoption, and about 4,000 children in British care were shipped to Australian institutions between 1945 and 1970. National apologies came in 2008 and 2013.

The Royal Commission of 2013 to 2017 heard that 4,444 people had reported abuse to Catholic authorities between 1980 and 2015. Between 2015 and 2018 every state and territory removed or changed the limitation period, the legal deadline to sue. Australia also sends demand abroad: about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled overseas in 2016, and in 2020 the bank Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty that included failing to check payments that could be linked to livestreamed child abuse in the Philippines.

When you read about an abuser in Australia, look at the list of postings, because each move was a decision by someone who knew. Ask who was told first and what they did next. The record here is detailed because a national Royal Commission examined churches, schools and state institutions together.

NLD.story:
In March 2010 the Catholic Church in the Netherlands set up a commission under former minister Wim Deetman. Its report of 16 December 2011 found at least 800 priests, monks and other religious had abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, with an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 minors abused. Bishops and officials had known. Their rule, the report said, was "not hanging out the dirty washing", meaning keep it inside the church and avoid scandal.

The Netherlands was also a large receiver of children from abroad. About 4,099 South Korean children were sent to Dutch families between 1969 and 2003, and about 4,000 babies came from Sri Lanka in the 1980s. A Dutch documentary in 2017 reported that many Sri Lankan babies were bought or taken from hospitals, handed to paid "acting mothers" who posed as birth mothers in court, and sold for adoption; Sri Lanka's health minister said on camera there were "a lot of baby farms back then". Greek-born children and children disappeared by El Salvador's army during its civil war were also adopted into the Netherlands. In February 2021 the Joustra committee found serious violations in adoptions from Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia and other countries between 1967 and 1998, and found Dutch officials had known for years and not stepped in. The government suspended all intercountry adoption on 8 February 2021, and in May 2024 announced citizens would no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad.

The country's role online is as host. For years the Netherlands held more of the abuse material removed by the Internet Watch Foundation than any other country: 47% in 2018, falling to 11%, or 33,788 web addresses, in 2025. In 2009 British police traced the "Boylover" forum's owner and server to the Netherlands; the follow-up operation identified 670 suspects, arrested 184 and safeguarded 230 children. Dutch police helped take down the Boystown platform, which had 400,000 registered users, in 2021. In 2013 the Dutch group Terre des Hommes ran "Sweetie", a sting using a fake Filipino child: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex in 10 weeks. Allegations in the Netherlands against Joris Demmink were investigated and never led to a charge; they remain unproven.

The Dutch record shows two kinds of looking away. One is a church protecting its name. The other is a government that approved adoption papers from abroad for decades without checking where the babies came from. When a country says it hosts abuse material, ask whether it is because the abusers are there, or because its cheap, fast internet hosting attracts people from everywhere.

IRL.story:
In 1975 two teenage boys were brought before a church inquiry in Ireland and made to swear oaths of silence about what Father Brendan Smyth, a Norbertine priest, had done to them. One of the men at those meetings, Seán Brady, later became a Cardinal. Their evidence never reached the police. The Norbertine order knew Smyth's history and moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries, including the United States, sometimes without warning the local bishop. The BBC counted at least 143 children abused. When police in Northern Ireland asked for his extradition, the Irish Attorney General's office delayed, and the row helped bring down the government in 1994. Smyth was jailed in Northern Ireland that year and in Dublin in 1997, and died in prison in August 1997.

The state inquiries that followed found the same habit across the country. The Ferns Report (2005) found Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests for a while and then put them back. The Murphy Report (2009) found four Dublin archbishops failed to tell the Gardaí, the police, what they knew; the archdiocese took out insurance against abuse claims from 1987; and the Gardaí knew of complaints against Father Tony Walsh in 1990–91 and did nothing. The Ryan Commission, which ran from 1999 to 2009, examined more than 250 church-run institutions that held over 30,000 children and found sexual abuse "endemic" in boys' institutions run mainly by the Christian Brothers. The Brothers sued in 2004 to keep their members' names out, and the report names no abusers. State school inspectors had visited and failed to stop it.

The Mother and Baby Homes Commission reported in January 2021. About 56,000 women and 57,000 children passed through the homes between 1922 and 1998, and about 9,000 children died there, roughly double the national infant death rate. The homes also worked as adoption agencies. In 2018 the state agency Tusla found 126 births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild agency, hiding who the children really were.

In 2000 Ireland gave survivors a one-year window to bring claims after the normal deadline had passed, and in 2017 gave its courts power to try Irish citizens for abuse committed anywhere in the world. Some abusers came back: Oliver O'Grady, convicted in California in 1993, was deported to Ireland in 2000 and convicted there in 2012 and 2020 over abuse images.

Ireland's inquiries came early and went deep, so its record is long. Notice that the same institutions show up in the abuse, the adoptions and the deaths, and that police, school inspectors and the Attorney General's office each had a chance to act. When an inquiry report names no one, ask who went to court to make that happen.

RUS.story:
From 1994 to 2014 the United States issued 60,266 immigrant visas to children adopted from Russia, with a peak of 5,865 in 2004. In total, 59,427 children were sent abroad from Russia between 2003 and 2022. In April 2010 an American adoptive mother put her 7-year-old adopted son alone on a one-way flight back to Moscow. On 28 December 2012 President Putin signed the Dima Yakovlev Law, banning adoption by US citizens from 1 January 2013. It was named after a Russian toddler who died in 2008 after his American adoptive father left him in a hot car; the father was found not guilty of involuntary manslaughter. The law was widely seen as a reply to the US Magnitsky Act, signed two weeks earlier, so the closure was about politics, not a finding of trafficking.

The children who stayed in Russia's own system had their own trouble. In 2014 Human Rights Watch visited 10 state orphanages for children with disabilities and found staff beating children, giving them sedative injections, sending them to psychiatric hospitals as punishment, and keeping the most disabled tied to cribs in "lying-down rooms". Children had almost no way to report it.

After February 2022 Russia began taking children from Ukraine. A decree of 30 May 2022 made it easier to give Ukrainian children Russian citizenship so Russian families could adopt them, and families were paid per child. Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. Yale researchers found at least 43 camps holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for "re-education". Ukraine's official count of deported children is 20,651. On 17 March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. The UN verified 122 abductions of children by Russian forces and authorities, and a UN commission found Russian forces committed rape and sexual violence, including against children.

Online, Moscow police asked US Customs for help in 2000 with Blue Orchid, a Moscow website selling videos of abused boys by mail; operators and customers were arrested in both countries. Russia hosted 5,797 web addresses of abuse material removed by the Internet Watch Foundation in 2025.

Russia's story shows a state on both sides: shutting one adoption route as a political move while running another out of a war zone. When a government says it is protecting children, check the dates, the numbers and who is doing the moving.

KHM.story:
In the early 1990s about 22,000 UN personnel arrived in Cambodia for the peacekeeping mission known as UNTAC. In two years the estimated number of sex workers rose from 6,000 to more than 25,000. The UN kept no proper record of abuse allegations at the time, and the sources consulted do not document findings about children against UNTAC staff.

By 2002 Svay Pak, a fishing village outside Phnom Penh, was known as a place where foreign men bought children, most of them ethnic Vietnamese girls sold by poor families. Observers linked its growth to Thailand's crackdown on child prostitution. On 22 January 2003 police raided Svay Pak. The raid had been announced in advance; nearly all the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville, and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had been taking money from brothel owners. The government shut the brothels in 2005, and the trade moved into massage parlours and karaoke bars. Estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers fell from nearly 35% to 1–2% by 2017.

Some of the buyers were caught by their own countries. Ronald Boyajian, already a registered sex offender in California, was arrested in Cambodia in 2009 on what prosecutors called his 35th trip to Asia; he was sentenced in the US to 70 years for abusing a nine-year-old girl in Svay Pak. A US official called Cambodia "ground zero for child sex tourism". Former Marine Michael Pepe was sentenced to 210 years in 2022.

Adoption was another route out. Between 1997 and 2001 the American facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid mothers for babies. The US stopped Cambodian adoptions in late 2001, and in 2004 Galindo pleaded guilty to visa fraud and money laundering, denying trafficking. Some families later found their child had living relatives. In 2019 the US State Department reported that some Cambodian orphanages bought children from poor families and kept them in poor conditions to attract donations. The 2025 report says children as young as 13 are held in brothels to pay family debts, and that official complicity, including at senior levels, blocks enforcement.

Cambodia shows how pressure in one country pushes the trade to the next, and how a raid can be emptied before it starts. When you hear that a place has "cleaned up", ask where the children were moved to, and who knew the date of the raid.

POL.story:
Between 1940 and 1945 the SS took children it judged "racially valuable" from occupied Poland, held them in Lebensborn homes and placed them with German families under new names. Estimates reported by DW run up to 200,000 Polish children; the map draws a flow of 20,000 to Germany. In 1947–48 a US military tribunal at Nuremberg tried 14 officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office and Lebensborn, convicted 13 and acquitted one.

Decades later the questions were about Poland's own church. In March 2019 the Polish bishops published a study counting 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. Two documentaries by the Sekielski brothers, "Tell No One" (May 2019, over 23 million YouTube views) and "Hide and Seek" (May 2020), showed bishops who had protected accused priests. The Vatican then investigated: Bishop Edward Janiak of Kalisz resigned in October 2020, Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź of Gdańsk was removed in August 2020 after covering up abuse by two priests, and Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz was disciplined in November 2020, ten days before he died.

Poland is also where two Polish clergymen accused of abuse in the Dominican Republic ended up. Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, the Pope's ambassador there, was recalled to the Vatican in August 2013, before Dominican prosecutors opened their case. The Vatican told Polish prosecutors its law did not allow his extradition. A Vatican prosecutor charged him in 2015, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms before trial. Father Wojciech Gil, who had worked in the Dominican Republic, came home to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic. Polish police arrested him in 2014 using Dominican evidence, and in March 2015 a court in Wołomin jailed him for seven years for abusing six minors there and two in Poland. So Poland both received an accused priest and prosecuted him.

In 2019 Poland created a State Commission on abuse of children under 15. In August 2022 it was criticised because church files sent to the Vatican were out of its reach, and church law has files destroyed ten years after a conviction. Poland still sends children abroad for adoption: 5,036 between 2003 and 2022.

When a church study gives a number, ask who counted and which files they could see. Poland's commission could not reach the documents held in Rome. The Gil case shows that a home country can still put someone on trial for abuse committed abroad when it chooses to.

THA.story:
In 1996 a Swiss man who had already been convicted of abusing children in Fribourg in 1980 and Valais in 1991 went back to Thailand. In Pattaya he ran a bar with a hotel room used by European men. Mainly between 2002 and 2013 he abused more than 80 boys there and in the northern village of Nong Hoi, and made boys perform acts with European clients. He was tried at home, not in Thailand: a Swiss court sentenced him to 16 years on 1 March 2018. A British former teacher and scout leader, Mark Frost, abused boys from poor families in Thailand in 2011–2013 and streamed the abuse to another European man; in 2017 a UK court gave him 13 life sentences. A British inquiry said it was one of only about eight successful UK prosecutions since 1997 for offences committed abroad.

Thailand tried to shut the door in the 1990s. A 1996 law made sex with anyone under 18 in a prostitution business a crime whatever the "consent", and a 2008 law targeted human trafficking. Observers reported that some of the trade moved next door to Cambodia. Thailand turned away 74 known foreign sex offenders at the border in 2017. Pressure came from the other side too: Australia said about 800 of its registered child sex offenders travelled abroad in 2016, often to Asia, and 40% did not tell police.

The trade did not end. In 2023 police raided an illegal bar on Bangla Road in Patong, Phuket, and freed six children under 18. In July 2024 a court sentenced seven people; the foreign owner, who had first fled to a neighbouring country, got 1,073 years in total. Five senior Patong police officers were transferred after the raid. The 2025 US trafficking report says children from Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos are increasingly trafficked for sex in brothels, bars, karaoke lounges and hotels.

Children also left Thailand. Between 2003 and 2022, 6,478 were sent abroad for adoption. In February 2011 police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held with their passports taken by a company called Baby 101 that took orders for newborns from childless couples; a Taiwanese woman was charged with trafficking. A former abbot known as the "jet-set monk", Wirapol, fled to the United States after 2013, was extradited in 2017 and convicted of abducting and raping a girl.

Notice how many of these cases were closed in Switzerland, Britain or the United States rather than in Thailand. A 2016 global study found most travelling offenders are regional or local travellers, not only Westerners. When police officers are moved after a raid, ask what they knew about the bar before it.

UGA.story:
From 1987 the Lord's Resistance Army, led by Joseph Kony, abducted children in northern Uganda and used them as fighters, porters and "wives". UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 had been taken by 2006. Some were held at LRA bases across the border in southern Sudan. One abducted child, Dominic Ongwen, grew up to command an LRA brigade. On 4 February 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted him of 61 crimes, including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage and using children under 15 as soldiers, and sentenced him to 25 years. Kony's ICC arrest warrant is still outstanding.

When adoption from Uganda to the United States grew, so did the money around it. US visas for children adopted from Kampala peaked at 277 in 2013, with 1,155 between 2005 and 2014. Between 2013 and 2016 an Ohio agency, European Adoption Consultants, arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children. Birth families were told their children would go to school in Kampala; the children were taken to an unlicensed home and then sent abroad. Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and officials to get adoption orders. A former employee pleaded guilty to bribery in 2019; in August 2020 two more employees and a Ugandan lawyer were charged, which means they are accused, not convicted. The same month the US government sanctioned two Ugandan judges, Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene, and two lawyers.

Ugandan soldiers sent to keep peace abroad are also in the record. In 2014 Human Rights Watch documented rapes and sexual exploitation by African Union soldiers in Mogadishu, Somalia, mainly by Ugandan and Burundian troops; the youngest victim was a 12-year-old girl allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier in May 2013. Many had come to the bases for medicine or food.

Inside Uganda, the 2025 US trafficking report says NGOs believe most child sex-trafficking victims are Karamojong, especially from Napak district. Traffickers, sometimes community elders, make children meet them at borders where markets are held to sell them into domestic work or sex, and rings move girls from Karamoja to Nairobi.

Uganda's record links war, adoption and peacekeeping, and in each one people with authority over children had a part: commanders, judges, soldiers, elders. When adoptions from one country rise fast, ask who is being paid along the way.

BRA.story:
Brazil has the largest Catholic population in the world, and no national inquiry into abuse in churches or children's institutions has been found in the sources reached. What is known came out one case at a time, through individual prosecutions and a 2010 parliamentary hearing about one priest. Countries such as Ireland, Australia and France held inquiries with the power to open files and survey the public; in France that approach found about 216,000 minors abused by clergy since 1950, against about 3,000 known before. Brazil has no figure like that, because no one has been given the job of counting.

On the coast, the pattern is tourism. In 2006 Brazil's Federal Police said sex tourism was most common in Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador and Natal, and ran raids such as one on a nightclub in Ponta Negra, Natal, where 110 foreigners were present and no children were found that night. A 2000 law set prison terms of 4 to 10 years for putting a child into prostitution. The 2025 US trafficking report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff in coastal tourist towns help arrange child sex trafficking, and cites a study suggesting up to 16 per cent of girls aged 14 to 17 in one northeastern metropolitan area were likely victims. It reports no investigations of complicit officials, and a 2016 case involving an elected official in Paraná was still unresolved.

Abusers also came in from far away. Warren Scott Kennell, an American missionary with New Tribes Mission, abused Katukina girls while posted in the Brazilian Amazon; he was arrested when he landed in Orlando and jailed for 58 years in 2014.

Children also left Brazil through adoption: 1,181 US visas for adopted Brazilian children between 1994 and 2014, and 5,456 children sent abroad between 2003 and 2022. In 2021 a Dutch inquiry found serious violations in adoptions from Brazil and other countries between 1967 and 1998.

Brazil's map entry is thin because the country has not looked, not because nothing happened. When a large country has no national inquiry, ask who would have to agree to one, and whose files it would open.

ETH.story:
In 2002, 262 Ethiopian children were adopted abroad. By 2008 the number was more than 3,887 a year. US visas for adopted Ethiopian children peaked at 2,514 in 2010, and 33,303 children were sent abroad between 2003 and 2022. As the numbers grew, Canadian families found their children's papers called them orphans when their parents were alive. The US State Department found one agency, Better Futures Adoption Services, involved in child trafficking, and it lost its Ethiopian licence in February 2011.

Receiving countries pulled out one by one. Ireland suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in October 2007, a Dutch agency stopped in September 2009, Australia stopped in December 2009, and Denmark in March 2016 after inspections. Ethiopia itself suspended foreign adoptions in November 2017 and in January 2018 its parliament banned adoption by foreigners, effective 18 February 2018. Lawmakers cited abuse and neglect of children abroad, after an American couple was convicted in 2013 over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl. The closing came from Ethiopia, years after the warnings began.

War brought a different harm. During the Tigray war that began in 2020, a UN-appointed commission of experts documented widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray, and rapes by Tigrayan forces of women and girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages such as Chenna in 2021. The BBC reported in February 2021 that 200 girls under 18 had registered at health centres in Mekelle as rape survivors. The UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia in 2024, 38 of them attributed to the national army.

Children are also trafficked out. The 2025 US trafficking report says organised begging rings exploit Ethiopian women and children in Saudi Arabia, and Ethiopian girls are held in domestic work and sex trafficking in Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes controlled with drugs. Reports of officials taking part continued.

Ethiopia shows how adoption can grow faster than anyone checks it, and how long it takes to close once doubts are raised. When a country's adoptions rise from hundreds to thousands in a few years, ask how many of those children really had no family.

MMR.story:
In 2012, at Buthidaung prison in Myanmar's Rakhine State, Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, were held and subjected to sexual violence. In 2017, during what the army called "clearance operations", hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped; in 80% of the cases UN investigators corroborated, it was a gang rape. The UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission reported in August 2019 that sexual violence was a "hallmark" of the army's operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan States. The army is the state's own armed force, so the people who would normally investigate are the ones accused.

The fighting kept taking children. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 85 children in Myanmar: 41 by the army and its allied militias, 33 by the Kachin Independence Army, mostly to make them fight. It verified the rape of two girls that year, one by each.

War also emptied villages, and the displaced became targets. In March 2019 Human Rights Watch reported that women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many living in displacement camps, were sold for US$3,000 to $13,000 to families in China, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. Traffickers were often relatives or acquaintances; one girl was sold at 16 by her sister-in-law. HRW said police in both Myanmar and China were "looking away", and the 2025 US trafficking report says displaced women and girls in Kachin and Shan are still at risk.

Abuse also happened in places meant to help children study. Up to 300,000 children may live in Myanmar's monasteries, TIME reported, with few records kept. At the Saitta Thuka monastery in Pathein, four girls aged 10 to 14, staying free so they could attend school, were repeatedly raped from June 2017 by the monk who ran the monastery, according to the children and families. When parents went to the police in early 2018 the monk disappeared. Police deferred to the religious affairs ministry and the monks' council, and an ex-monk who had reprimanded him was told to move away.

Myanmar's cases show what happens when the people with power over children, soldiers or monks, answer to no outside authority. When a report says police "deferred" to someone, ask who that was and what they did with the case.

SSD.story:
In Malakal, South Sudan, displaced people live in a camp run by the UN, called a Protection of Civilians site. In September 2022 an investigation by The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022 aid workers there exploited displaced women and girls, trading aid for sex; women and girls said they were raped and became pregnant. Staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named. These are reports by journalists, not court findings.

The army is the largest abuser in the UN's count. In 2022 the UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls in South Sudan, some as young as 7. Of those, 74 were attributed to the national army, the South Sudan People's Defence Forces; others to opposition factions (14 in total) and 2 to the national police. In 2024 the UN verified 7 cases, 5 by the army. Years earlier, the Lord's Resistance Army held children it had abducted from northern Uganda at bases in southern Sudan.

When peacekeepers are accused, the decision to punish rests with the soldier's home country, not South Sudan or the UN. The UN's 2025 report on peacekeeper abuse lists few cases finished: one Togolese officer was sent home and given 60 days in prison, while others sit "pending additional information from the member state".

Very little of what happens to children here reaches the international reporting systems. In 2025 the US tip line for online child abuse, NCMEC's CyberTipline, received 863 reports for South Sudan, out of 23.4 million worldwide. That is not a sign of safety. It reflects a country with few connections, few investigators and few ways to report.

South Sudan's record comes mostly from UN monitors and reporters, because local courts and police rarely act. When the people who are supposed to protect children are the ones accused, ask who has the power to try them, and whether that country has ever used it.

PAN.story:
In early 2021 a subcommission of Panama's National Assembly reported cases of abuse in shelters for children at social risk. These shelters, called albergues, were run by private groups and NGOs but supervised by the state's children's agency, Senniaf. By March 2021 prosecutors had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and found 20 victims, who were moved. Five people were charged, with offences including child mistreatment, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters checked, found 70% of 44 shelters lacked suitable staff, and said Senniaf did little follow-up.

Panama also appears on routes run from other countries. In Cartagena, Colombia, Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello, known as "La Madame", supplied young women and minors to parties on yachts and in hotels and sent women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas, coaching them to avoid scrutiny at airports. In 2018 she accepted trafficking and conspiracy charges in a plea deal and got eight years and one month. At hearings she threatened to name politicians and powerful men she said were clients; that is her claim and has not been verified.

Online, the trail runs through Panama too. In October 2024 police arrested a man in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera, accused of contacting children through the Roblox game and threatening them to get abuse images. The tip came from Spanish police. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation removed 5,275 web addresses of abuse material hosted in Panama, 2% of its total.

When a government pays others to care for children, the question is who checks on them. Panama's numbers came out because legislators and the Ombudsman went and looked; ask how often those visits happen when no one is asking.

TCD.story:
In October 2007, in Abéché in eastern Chad, members of a French charity called Zoé's Ark were stopped as they tried to fly 103 children to host families in France. The charity said the children were orphans from Darfur in neighbouring Sudan. Chadian authorities found most were from Chad and were not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children, sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each child. A Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years, and two Chadians were acquitted. The six French members were sent to France, and at the end of March 2008 Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them.

The case shows how a war next door can be used to call children "orphans" so they can be moved. Chad then closed this route.

Chad's own army appears in the UN's records. In 2022 the UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province, and in Sudan attributed 4 of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 to Chadian soldiers. In the Lake Chad area it verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa.

Beyond these cases, little is measured. Childlight's 2026 study found that West and Central Africa, where Chad sits, has no representative surveys of children about online sexual abuse, so no one knows how common it is there.

Chad's record is a few clear cases surrounded by gaps. When a charity says children are orphans from a war zone, ask who checked and whether their families were found. When a country has no survey data, a short list of cases tells you how little has been looked at, not how little happened.

GIN.story:
In 2001–2002 a joint team from the UN refugee agency UNHCR and Save the Children UK looked at refugee camps in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Its report in early 2002 said refugee children were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, by peacekeepers and by community leaders, often in exchange for food and aid.

The UN's internal investigators, the Office of Internal Oversight Services, then looked into 43 cases fully and substantiated 10. Among them were the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a camp in Guinea and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou. One substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was sent home. In October 2002 the investigators said no allegation against a UN staff member had been substantiated and that they found no evidence of "widespread" abuse. Save the Children UK answered that nothing the UN had found made it think it was wrong. The two reports describe the same camps very differently, and the gap between 43 cases examined and 10 proven is part of the story.

Since then, little has been measured in Guinea. Childlight's 2026 study found West and Central Africa has no representative surveys of children about online sexual abuse, so there is no estimate of how common it is.

Guinea's case is about what happens when the people giving out aid are also the people children must report to. When an organisation investigates its own staff and finds nothing widespread, ask who else was allowed to look, and how many children were able to speak to someone outside the camp.

MWI.story:
In 2006 police in Slovenia detained a Catholic priest, Father Franc Frantar, over the abuse of up to 16 minors. Instead of facing trial at home, he went to Malawi as a missionary. He came back to Slovenia only after Interpol issued a notice for him.

Today the record in Malawi centres on Dzaleka, a refugee camp built for 10,000 people that holds about 53,000. The 2025 US trafficking report says organised crime groups working from informal bars and housing in the camp recruit girls for sex trafficking, inside the camp and in roadside bars along the highway to the capital, Lilongwe. The camp is a stop on the "Southern Route" that moves migrants towards South Africa, where some end up in sex trafficking or forced labour. Girls are also exploited in bars and illegal brothels in Lilongwe and Blantyre. The report says officials taking part in or protecting the trade continued to block enforcement.

Malawi shows two ways a poor country becomes a destination: an abuser sent from abroad to escape a court, and a crowded camp where children have no one to turn to. When you read that a priest went abroad as a missionary after police took an interest, ask who approved the posting and whether anyone in the new country was told.

SVN.story:
In 2006 police in Slovenia detained Father Franc Frantar, a Catholic priest, over the abuse of up to 16 minors. He did not stay for trial. He left for Malawi in southern Africa to work as a missionary, out of reach of Slovenian prosecutors. He returned only after Interpol, the international police network, issued a notice for him. The map draws this as one of 34 documented cases in which an accused abuser was moved or went abroad instead of being stopped.

Slovenia also appears in an older record. During the Second World War, Nazi Germany's SS seized children judged "racially valuable" in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn homes and placed them with German families under new identities. In 1947–48 a US military tribunal at Nuremberg tried 14 officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office and Lebensborn over the kidnapping of children; it convicted 13 and acquitted one. The map marks Slovenia as one of the places involved.

Slovenia's entries are few. When a priest under investigation is posted to a mission abroad, ask who in the church signed off on it and whether the receiving country was warned. A short list of cases can mean little has been examined.

XKX.story:
In 1999 NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in Kosovo. Soon after, Kosovo became a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution. Amnesty International's May 2004 report said the international presence, soldiers of the NATO force KFOR, UN police and international staff, produced 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia, and local girls were abducted too.

The same year, the UN's own peacekeeping department admitted that peacekeepers had "come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution". Amnesty found no evidence that any soldier had faced criminal proceedings in his home country. Under the rules for foreign troops, only the soldier's own country can put him on trial, so the people paying for the trade were mostly beyond the reach of Kosovo's courts.

Kosovo's case shows how a large group of foreign men with money and legal protection can create a market that traffickers then supply. When an international mission arrives somewhere, ask what rules its people follow, which country would try them for a crime, and whether that country ever has.

COG.story:
Between September and December 2015 a contingent of soldiers from the Republic of Congo guarded the airport at Bambari, in the Central African Republic, as part of the UN peacekeeping mission there, MINUSCA. In January 2016 Human Rights Watch researchers in Bambari documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by peacekeepers. They included a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near the airport. Survivors believed the soldiers were from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo, and HRW linked the airport cases to the Republic of Congo contingent. These are findings by a rights group, not by a court.

Under UN rules, a peacekeeper accused of a crime can be tried only by his own country. So whether these cases were ever prosecuted is a question for Congo-Brazzaville, not for the Central African Republic or the UN. The map marks Congo-Brazzaville as the home country of accused troops.

Inside the country, there is little data. Childlight's 2026 study found West and Central Africa has no representative surveys of children about online sexual abuse.

When soldiers are sent abroad to protect civilians, the country that sends them also holds the power to punish them. Ask whether Congo-Brazzaville reported back on these cases, and what happened to the soldiers who guarded Bambari airport.

ISL.story:
Iceland appears on this map mainly as a place where servers sit. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British group that finds and removes child abuse material online, took down 7,455 web addresses hosted in Iceland, 2% of everything it removed that year. A server is the computer that stores a website; the people uploading and watching may be anywhere in the world.

The map links Iceland to two large international police operations in 2025. In the first, Operation Stream, Bavarian police led 38 countries and Europol against Kidflix, a paid site created in 2021 that let 1.8 million users stream or download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency. 91,000 unique videos were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized its server on 11 March 2025; 1,393 suspects were identified and 79 were arrested; the case record counts 39 children. Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history. In the second, Operation Cumberland, Danish police and 18 other countries went after a platform selling AI-generated abuse material made by a Danish man arrested in November 2024; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol noted that many countries had no law covering images made by AI. Those arrested in both operations are charged, not convicted.

A small, quiet country can still carry a share of the world's abuse material because hosting is cheap and fast. When you see a country on a list of hosts, ask which companies rent out the servers and how quickly they act on a removal notice.

MNG.story:
In Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia's capital, and in provincial towns and border areas, the 2025 US trafficking report says women and girls are trafficked for sex in hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs. It says this is sometimes made easier because police do not enforce the law, and that some families take part. Traffickers also use online platforms to groom children, building trust before asking for images, and then blackmail them with what they have sent. Children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, for example as horse jockeys.

This is the only case on the map for Mongolia, and it comes from a foreign government's yearly report rather than a Mongolian court or inquiry.

When the main source for a country is an outside report, the picture is a summary, not a count. Ask whether Mongolia's own police have opened cases against the hotels and clubs named, and what happens when an officer is the one looking away.

JAM.story:
In 2023 a study in Jamaica estimated that 6.3 per cent of children aged 12 to 17 had lived through conditions that point to trafficking. The 2025 US trafficking report, which cites that study, says children are trafficked for sex in resort areas visited by tourists, sometimes with a parent involved, and that in some communities men pay girls or their families for sex. Those named as part of the trade include family members, local power brokers and both foreign and local buyers.

The report says corruption and the involvement of officials, including in law enforcement, remain serious concerns. When the police are part of the problem, a child or family has few safe places to report.

Jamaica's 6.3 per cent figure is a survey estimate, which is more than many countries have. Ask who buys in the resort towns, and what happens to an officer accused of protecting the trade.

LUX.story:
Between 1984 and 2008, 561 South Korean children were sent to Luxembourg for adoption. They were part of about 163,898 children South Korea sent abroad from 1953 to 2008. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state had enabled fraud in these overseas adoptions: agencies sent children in set numbers to meet foreign demand, and some children with known parents were registered as orphans. Luxembourg is on the map as a receiving country, where those children grew up.

No other case for Luxembourg is recorded here. Its part in this story is quiet but real: each adoption needed approval at both ends.

If you know someone adopted from Korea in those years, their papers may not tell the whole truth about where they came from. Ask whether Luxembourg has checked its own adoption files, as the Netherlands did in 2021.

CRI.story:
In 2018 a Costa Rican Catholic priest, Father Mauricio Víquez, fled the country as abuse accusations against him came out. He went through Panama to Mexico. He was caught there and extradited, meaning handed back by one country to another for trial, in 2021. In 2022 a Costa Rican court sentenced him to 20 years.

The map counts this among 34 documented cases in which an accused abuser was moved or left the country rather than being stopped at the first report. In this case the flight did not work: two countries cooperated and he was returned and tried.

Costa Rica's record here is one case. When someone accused of abusing children leaves the country, ask how they were able to leave, who helped, and whether the other country is willing to send them back.

STP.story:
There are no documented cases for São Tomé and Príncipe on this map, and that absence is the story. Childlight's 2026 update, which measures online sexual exploitation of children, rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries. West and Central Africa, where São Tomé and Príncipe sits, has none, so no one has measured how often children there are abused or exploited online.

The gap is wider than one survey. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline, the main global tip line for online child abuse, could not be placed in any country at all. The map's record is thickest where people looked.

A blank country is not a safe country. Ask whether anyone has surveyed children there, whether police have a unit for these crimes, and where reports would go if a child made one.

DZA.story:
There are no documented cases for Algeria on this map, and that absence is the story. Childlight's 2026 update, which measures online sexual exploitation of children, rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries. The Middle East and North Africa, which includes Algeria, has none, so there is no measure of how often children there are abused or exploited online.

Other global counts have holes too. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline, the main global tip line for online child abuse, could not be placed in any country. The map's documented record is thickest where people looked.

A blank on the map reflects missing data, not missing abuse. Ask whether Algeria has surveyed children, whether it reports trafficking data to the UN, and what a child there can do to report abuse.

MDV.story:

South Asia, which includes the Maldives, has none, so there is no measure of how often children there are abused or exploited online.

Other global records are incomplete too. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023. A country with no cases on the map is a country where the questions have not been asked in a way that produces numbers. Ask who would run a survey of children there, and where a report of abuse would go.
